content:
Hi everyone - We are developing a Lean game for an introductory proofs course and are hoping to use it as a substantial part of the course rather than just as an optional activity.

We have a server on which we can self-host lean4game. What we would also like, though, is a way for students to log in and for us to persist their progress server-side: e.g. which levels they have completed, perhaps their submitted proofs/attempts, timestamps, and probably some basic instructor-facing progress information.

As far as I can tell, this is not something provided by Lean's language-server interface itself, which is presumably the wrong layer for authentication or persistent application state anyway. And the standard lean4game setup appears to store game progress in browser local storage rather than associating it with an authenticated user account.

Has anyone already built a layer around lean4game that provides authentication and server-side persistence of student progress? Or is there another Lean-based teaching platform/project that would be a better starting point for this use case?

If not, I'm also interested in architectural advice. My current thought is to leave Lean/lean4game responsible for the interactive proving experience and put authentication, a database, and progress/event logging in a separate web application layer around it. Is that roughly the right approach, or are there hooks in lean4game that would make this substantially easier?

I've found the previous discussions here about self-hosting Lean for students, automatic grading, and building one's own Lean game, but I haven't found one specifically about authenticated, persistent per-student game progress. Apologies if I've missed it!
I'm not aware of any progress on this, but if you have some electronic learning environment (e.g. Moodle), doing LTI-integration might be the way to go.

Sorry for the late reply, but the basic answer is no – lean4game does not offer any inbuilt support for user authentication. There are two reasons for this: (a) I conceived of the Lean Game Server as a hack that delivers Lean to students in a way that bypasses university curricula, and (b) our university is paranoid about GDPR.
